Subverting
the Tracks

Refugee Agency and the 1943 Feldkirch Freight Train Escape

The story of a group of Jewish refugees who sought a route to safety through a freight train, and of the history of resistance that railway landscapes can reveal.

Research and text: Marie JensenFirst Cycle · 2026
Begin the exhibition ↓
Feldkirch, Austria7 January 1943Jewish refugee agency
The central question
How does the forgotten history of the 1943 freight train escape redefine our understanding of active refugee resistance, and how does shifting our lens to this Austrian border node challenge the German-centric biases of mainstream Holocaust education?

01

Railways, deportation and a different perspective

The European rail network played a vital role in the Nazis’ “Final Solution” against European Jews. Using both freight and passenger cars, German authorities transported millions of people to killing centers in German-occupied Poland and the occupied Soviet Union. Many Holocaust survivors’ oral histories describe conditions on the trains, including little or no food and water, extreme temperatures depending on the season, and a lack of sanitation (United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, “German Railways and the Holocaust”).

Although the railway was crucial to the Nazis’ plan, and it is vital to teach the horrors of the “Final Solution,” Holocaust education has often conditioned the public to view train cars solely as vehicles of victimhood. Looking at an incident in Feldkirch, Austria, reveals a narrative of subversion and resistance in which refugees attempted to reclaim control over the tracks in their struggle for survival. This example may also help Holocaust education move beyond a German-centric perspective and allow lesser-known narratives to be heard.

02

The border under surveillance

In 1938, as asylum requests from German Jews increased, Switzerland began negotiations with Nazi Germany in the hope of limiting the number of Jewish refugees entering the country (St. Louis Kaplan Feldman Holocaust Museum). Fueled by antisemitism, the Reich Ministry of the Interior invalidated German passports held by Jews on 5 October 1938. The German government increasingly required Jews to identify themselves in ways that distinguished them from the rest of the population.

German Jews were required to carry identity cards, passports were stamped with a red letter “J,” and Jews whose first names were considered to be of “non-Jewish” origin were required to add “Israel” or “Sara” (United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, “German Jews’ Passports Declared Invalid”). These measures intensified the surveillance and restrictions that Jews were actively resisting, forcing refugees to seek other routes of escape.

03

7 January 1943: the freight train escape

One such attempt to evade increased surveillance at the borders took place on 7 January 1943 in Feldkirch, a small Austrian town near Switzerland. Fourteen Jewish refugees were discovered on a coal train after officials became suspicious of the overloaded wagon SZ 17068, whose sliding door could not be opened. Main customs assistant Reithmeyer recorded in the chronicle of the Feldkirch main customs office that the refugees had covered their faces with scarves against the frost and cold and were wearing several layers of clothing. He also noted that they resisted but were eventually forced to crawl out from beneath the coal at gunpoint.

According to the account, when questioned in detail, the refugees explained that they had boarded the wagons in Slovakia on 30 December 1942 in order to avoid being deported to a labor camp (Loewy, “Slovakian Jews — January 7, 1943”). This incident, along with other efforts such as an escape organization in Medzilaborce that helped Jews attempting to reach Switzerland, offers a documented example of Jewish resistance within the railway system at the Austrian–Swiss border. Focusing on a lesser-known Austrian town, instead of only the major cities that often dominate Holocaust education, expands our understanding of the many cities and countries involved.

Curatorial note · Reading the evidence

The event is documented through the Feldkirch customs-office chronicle, as presented by the Crossing the Border project. This is an official record of the refugees’ discovery and arrest, not a first-person testimony. The attempted escape should not be mistaken for a successful border crossing. The photographs in this exhibition were taken in May and June 2026; they show the present-day landscape, not the events of 1943.

04

Teaching histories of resistance

Acts of resistance that occurred in small border towns are often absent from classrooms. When these histories are not included, important examples of Jewish resourcefulness and agency are erased. Holocaust education must challenge the passive-victim stereotype by showing that the railways were also spaces of Jewish agency and attempted escape across borders.

There have been calls for teachers to educate students about Jewish resistance during the Holocaust through memoirs and documented events that focus on its different forms. One teacher at a Jewish day school stressed the importance and prevalence of different forms of resistance during the Holocaust; other teachers likewise rejected the idea that students should leave the classroom believing Jews went passively to their deaths (Ellison).

Looking at lesser-known histories, such as the events in Feldkirch, sheds light on often-overlooked acts of physical resistance. It also helps to show that the Holocaust was part of a wider European history, while emphasizing the importance of sharing marginalized voices and experiences.

About the project

In the author’s words

Marie Jensen’s original project framing is presented alongside the exhibition narrative.

The story

The forgotten history of the 1943 Feldkirch freight train escape reveals a German-centric gap in Holocaust education. The incident brings to light a narrative of active subversion within an intense surveillance network. Its limited visibility in mainstream Holocaust education calls for a digital public-history intervention that challenges the passive-victim stereotype and situates the Holocaust in a wider, interconnected history.

Where and when?

My story is situated in Feldkirch, Austria, in 1943. It focuses on the group of refugees who attempted to escape into Switzerland on a freight train passing through Feldkirch. My main audience is Holocaust educators, museum curators, and students learning about the Holocaust.

Why does this story matter?

Mainstream Holocaust education has often conditioned the public to view the railway system only as a vehicle of victimhood. I argue that looking at a small city such as Feldkirch, and the acts of resistance that occurred there, can show public audiences that the Holocaust was not exclusively a German historical event. These marginalized stories also reveal moments of resistance.
